before: —hard for outsiders to accept)—and they call wrath anger as it begins. Scripture often marks a difference between wrath and anger, as in "Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger." We do not define God's rebuking wrath the same way as the wrath we must cast off, nor the Lord's disciplining anger the same as ours. Speech about God is more figurative; what is named in us is plainly passion and sin.

Bitterness also appears in Jeremiah: "Your bitterness rose up before me." In Paul I take bitterness as we call people bitter rather than sweet—custom knows both. Wrath is anger starting in the soul toward someone. Anger here is not merely the genus of such feelings, but anger already primed and active to punish the one thought to have done wrong. Clamor usually rides with them: the bitter, wrathful, and angry shout and speak more noisily, pouring out words of bitterness, wrath, and anger. So clamor too must be practiced away.

Blasphemy to be removed is, I think, what the angry often utter when, from passion, they even dare to speak against God—when every charge about anything is swept into blasphemy. People "blaspheme" when they speak evil of those they speak evil of. So after bitterness, wrath, anger, and clamor, blasphemy too must be put off.

If we also take blasphemy as every voice that speaks badly of the divine—not only from grief and anger when people are displeased, but often from ignorance of the truth, as heterodox doctrines show—then whoever calls the true word false or the false true also blasphemes, especially about God and God's matters. Who is so approved a money-changer as to test all things, hold the good, and abstain from every form of evil?

Some think anger can be reasonable, and they insert "without cause" into the gospel saying that whoever is angry with his brother is liable to judgment. Shame them with this text: "Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be taken from you." Here "all" covers everything: no bitterness allowed, no wrath permitted, no anger excused as reasonable. Psalm 36 says, as if all anger (and wrath) were sin, "Cease from anger and forsake wrath." So it is never right to be angry with anyone. Labor to strip not only all bitterness, wrath, anger, and blasphemy, but these together with all malice—malice as the habit opposite virtue, or as wickedness.

[[Ephesians 4:32 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:32]] "Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving yourselves as God in Christ also forgave you." We called the opposite of bitter "sweet"; Paul names kindness as bitterness's opposite, by a food metaphor. So "be kind to one another" means be approachable, sweet in character, and gentle. That comes when we put off raw, merciless, unsympathetic ways toward the neighbor and become tenderhearted to all—and by that we grant the greatest gifts not only to others but to ourselves.

"Forgiving yourselves" is not the same as "forgiving one another." Whatever good we do in benefiting others returns more to us—by the end and by our being under the law—than to those we seem to help. We grant ourselves what God granted us in Christ when we receive it, keep it, and imitate the Giver and his way of giving. Another reader, thinking "forgiving yourselves" no different from "forgiving one another," continues in the next section.

Another, presenting the ranking by which God ranks each into some order, will say this: he subjected under his feet all things that belong to the order of those who are being subjected. And he gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all. Finding the church called Christ’s body, we ask whether, as the rest of the body beside the head, one must think it an instrument of the head, or as a human body of which the head is a part, so Christ’s body is the whole church of Christ, ensouled by his deity and filled by his Spirit—or whether these things must be taken otherwise. If the second is so, his more human side will itself also be a part of the whole body, while the divine and life-giving of the whole church will be the divine power that as it were ensouls it. And we want to know how the church, being Christ’s body, is the fullness of him who fills all in all, and why it is not said “of him who fills all in all” but “of him who is filled.” For it will seem more consistent to have said that Christ is the one who fills, not the one filled; for he is not only fullness of law but fullness of all fullnesses, nothing becoming full apart from him. See whether one can answer thus: just as through the Son’s great relation and fellowship with the rational beings the Son of God is as it were fullness of all rational beings, so also he himself as it were takes fullness into himself, being most fully revealed in each of the blessed. And to make the saying clearer, think of a king filled with the kingdom in each who increase the kingdom, and emptied of it in those who withdraw; and nothing fits Christ’s philanthropic kingship better than this king, each of those who fill it out being benefited by him rationally and perfected, who, fleeing to him, fill out his body, somehow empty when the benefited are lacking. Therefore Christ is filled in all who approach, lacking them before they come.

Ephesians 2:1–5: “And you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit now working in the sons of disobedience, among whom we all also once conducted ourselves in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, as the rest also; but God, being rich in mercy because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.” The sequence is: and you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins, God made alive together with Christ, being rich in mercy because of the great love with which he loved us; and even when we were dead in trespasses, in which we once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit now working in the sons of disobedience, among whom we all also once conducted ourselves in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, he made us alive together with Christ. The connective “but God, being rich in mercy” we think either has been inserted uselessly in the copies or, as by an unskilled hand, was not seen as redundant beside Paul’s wording. And sins are clearly said to be death of the soul, from “and you being dead in your trespasses and your sins.” And since “trespass” is a name proper to Scripture, one must examine whether it differs from “sin,” especially since here they are woven together: “dead in your trespasses and your sins.” And we ask whether the evils already finished by us are called our “sins,” while their beginnings, not yet falls but journeying toward our falling, are “trespasses.” And perhaps for this reason Psalm 18 says, “Who will understand trespasses?”—because the one who understands the roots and beginnings of sins that are “trespasses” would also be able to guard himself so as not to fall under the “sins” as well.
